## Suicide-related recommendations, 2024 vs. 2025

**No. By this measure, suicide prevention shrank sharply as an OIG theme from 2024 to 2025.** But the drop probably comes partly from changes in how OIG inspects, not only from changes in the problem.

Data as of **2026-11-04**. The data is current, and it matches OIG's dashboard within tolerance.

| Year | Reports with a recommendation mentioning "suicide" | Suicide recommendations | All reports with recommendations | Share of reports |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 | **56** | 98 (all closed as implemented) | 155 | ~36% |
| 2025 | **11** | 19 (13 closed as implemented, 6 open) | 132 | ~8% |

The total number of reports dropped only about 15%. The number of reports with a suicide recommendation dropped about 80%. So the decline is not just because OIG published fewer reports.

## What these counts can show
- How often OIG's written recommendations used the word "suicide" each year, both as a raw number and as a share of all reports with recommendations.
- How well VA followed through. Every 2024 suicide recommendation was closed as implemented, with a median of about 232 days to closure. None of the 2025 recommendations has been closed as "not implemented."

## What they cannot show
- **Whether suicide risk or VA's suicide prevention got better or worse.** A falling count could mean facilities improved. It could also mean OIG changed its inspection methods, changed what it focused on, or published fewer reports. The data can't tell these apart.
- **Program changes are the likely explanation.** Splitting 2024–2025 by report type:
  - Most suicide recommendations (55) came from the **Comprehensive Healthcare Inspection Program**, which OIG has since replaced with the Healthcare Facility Inspection program. That newer program produced **no** recommendations mentioning suicide in this period.
  - The rest came from Vet Center inspections (20), hotline inspections (20), mental health inspections (11) and national reviews (11).
  
  So much of the drop probably reflects the program switch: the old program apparently reviewed suicide prevention routinely at facilities. The switch itself is my inference. The data shows which programs produced these recommendations, but it does not document why the switch happened.
- **How much attention OIG gave the topic overall.** Reports can discuss suicide in their findings without a recommendation using that word. Reports with no recommendations, or with every element passing, are not counted.
- **Recommendations worded differently.** I searched only for the word "suicide," so recommendations that say "suicidal," "safety plan," "lethal means" or similar may be missed.
- **Two years is not a trend.** Without earlier years and data from after 2025, it's hard to call this a long-term direction.
- **Small gaps from OIG's records.** The dataset has about 129 fewer recommendations than OIG's own total. That gap is within tolerance and is unlikely to change the picture.

## Open items
Six of the 2025 recommendations were still open as of the data date: 3 from Vet Center inspections, 2 from mental health inspections and 1 from a national review. One mental health item and the national review item, and possibly some Vet Center items, may be from 2024 reports. The Vet Center items and the national review item have been open for more than a year.

**Next steps I can take:** count earlier years for a longer trend, add terms like "suicidal" or "safety plan," or list the specific reports with report numbers and links.

**The most common recurring finding is about how facilities communicate test results, and it appears in 21 of 112 reports in scope (about 19%). El Paso is not in that group.** Data as of 2026-11-04; the dataset is not marked stale.

**The finding:** OIG recommends that the Chief of Staff and the Associate Director for Patient Care Services write workflows showing each team member's part in communicating test results. This is required by VHA Directive 1088(1), *Communicating Test Results to Providers and Patients*.
- 26 recommendations across 21 reports, all cited in 2026.
- 17 of the 26 are still open.
- The median time to close is 0 days, but only 9 closed items have timing data. Items closed on the day a report comes out pull that number down, so it doesn't show a typical closure time.

**The same issue also shows up in a separate group.** A differently worded recommendation about test-result policies, workflows and patient-notification monitoring appears in 12 of 112 reports (2025–2026), with a median of 256 days to close. Some reports may be in both groups, so the two counts can't simply be added. Even so, test-result communication is clearly the biggest recurring issue in the current program.

Next most common, for context:
- Keeping a clean environment to reduce infection risk: 11 of 112
- Stable facility leadership, a recommendation to the VISN Director: 9 of 112
- Keeping patient care areas clean and safe: 9 of 112

**El Paso (station 756, VISN 17)**
- None of El Paso's recommendations fall in either test-results group. Its Healthcare Facility Inspection ([25-00193-155](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system), published 2026-07-16) made only two recommendations, and both are open:
  1. Executive leaders make sure staff keep the environment clean and safe (target date: Jan. 29, 2027). This matches the cleanliness theme above, in a different group.
  2. Providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days (target date: Dec. 31, 2026).
- The report does cite VHA Directive 1088(1) on page 14, so OIG looked at test-result communication there, but it made no recommendation on it.
- **Estimated next inspection: around January 2028.** This is only an estimate (the last inspection ended 2025-01-16, plus OIG's roughly three-year cycle). OIG doesn't publish a schedule.

**Caveats from the tool:**
- A group gathers recommendations with matching or similar wording. It points to a shared issue but doesn't prove a common cause. One topic can be split across several groups, so a single group isn't a full count for that topic.
- These groups are ranked by how often they appear, not by how serious they are, and they don't predict what an inspection will find. The tool doesn't rate facilities.
- "Not in this group" only means none of El Paso's recommendations were sorted into that group. It doesn't mean El Paso was never cited for the topic.

Here are two examples of what facilities committed to do after OIG cited them for unsecured medication carts. Both recommendations are now **closed-implemented**. The data is current as of **2026-11-04** and isn't stale.

**Example 1: Orlando VA Medical Center, Orlando, FL. Report 14-00689-142 (published 2014-05-06)**
- **Recommendation:** Strengthen processes so medication and supply carts are secured at all times, and monitor compliance.
- **What the facility committed to do:**
  - Nursing, Medical and Surgical Services worked together on the fix. Everyone using the carts, including nurses and providers, must lock them before leaving an exam room.
  - Nurse managers reviewed the process one-on-one with nursing staff on March 26, 2014. An email to all nursing and provider staff followed on April 2, 2014, setting a 100% compliance requirement.
  - Service chiefs planned more training for providers and residents.
  - Nurse managers would make random, unannounced checks of all carts until compliance stayed at 90% or higher for 3 months in a row.
- **Status:** Closed-implemented on 2014-09-25.
- Link: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-orlando-va-0

**Example 2: Atlanta VA Medical Center, Decatur, GA. Report 13-03653-91 (published 2014-03-12)**
- **Recommendation:** Strengthen processes so medication carts are secured at all times, and monitor compliance.
- **What the facility committed to do:** Atlanta's problem was partly equipment, since some carts had locks that didn't work.
  - Carts with broken locks were being repaired or replaced. Six new carts had arrived, 26 more were on order, and the rest were being purchased.
  - Until then, carts were kept in a locked medication room unless in use.
  - The BCMA (bar code medication administration) coordinator would do regular rounds of all inpatient areas to check and record compliance.
- **Target date:** December 31, 2014.
- **Status:** Closed-implemented on 2015-03-11.
- Link: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-atlanta-va-1

**The common approach:** Most responses combine retraining staff, fixing or replacing carts with broken locks, and audits until a set compliance level is reached. Other facilities' responses look similar:
- **West Palm Beach (15-00071-158):** daily nurse manager rounds and tracking through environment of care (EOC) rounds.
- **San Francisco (15-00607-483):** told staff to lock carts by hand rather than rely on the automatic timed lockout.
- **Palo Alto (13-00279-156):** monthly audits on every shift until 100% compliance.

**Limitation:** These examples come from 2013–2016 reviews under OIG's older inspection program. They're the top search results, not a full count of every time OIG has cited unsecured medication carts.

# OIG inspection prep: VA El Paso Healthcare System (Station 756, VISN 17)

**Data as of 2026-11-04.** The data is current (not stale) and matches OIG's published counts.

## 1. When the next inspection might come (estimate only)
- **Estimated window: around January 2028.** This is my estimate, not a schedule. I added about three years to your last inspection, because OIG says it inspects on a roughly three-year cycle. OIG doesn't publish dates, so an inspection could come sooner.
- Your last inspection was a Healthcare Facility Inspection that ended 2025-01-16. The report came out 2026-07-16: [25-00193-155](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system).

## 2. Your own open recommendations (4 of 66; start here)

| # | Recommendation | Report | Target | What to do now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Executive leaders keep the environment clean and safe | [25-00193-155](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system), rec 1 | 2027-01-29 | Keep records of each piece of the plan: restroom cleaning logs, rounds by the EMS tech, the 24 cleaning SOPs, training records from June 2, 2026, daily checks by the EMS Chief, and weekly EOC rounds by the Associate Director. |
| 2 | Providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days | same report, rec 2 | **2026-12-31 (under 2 months away)** | Your plan says the SOP was still "under development," so check that it's finished. Your stated goal is **zero overdue screenings for six months in a row**, reported monthly to the CEC starting June 2026. Make sure each of those months is documented for the closure request. |
| 3 | Video surveillance working and monitored in the data center | [23-01179-204](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/information-security-inspection/inspection-information-security-va-el-paso-healthcare) (info security, published 2023-09-27), rec 5 | none on record | This is assigned to OIT and has been open **more than 3 years**. No corrective action is on record in this data. Ask your local OIT lead for a status update. |
| 4 | Water detection sensors installed in the data center | same report, rec 7 | none on record | Same as #3. |

**Other issues in the last report that OIG noted without a recommendation.** OIG didn't make recommendations on these because you showed fixes by December 2025. Inspectors may still check that the fixes held:
- Clean and dirty items stored together in the soiled utility rooms of the primary care and women's health clinics. Your fix: separate rooms and monthly checks.
- Expired respirator masks in a locked storage room that EOC rounds had skipped for six months. Your fix: the EOC team now has access to all spaces.
- An emergency alert system at an outpatient clinic that only a police officer could reset. Your fix: the reset was moved to a corridor nursing staff can reach.
- A damaged women's restroom floor, which the VISN had also flagged in FY2024. Your fix: the floor was repaired, with yearly checks.

**Repeat findings:** None. The tool counts a repeat when the same standard recommendation appears in more than one of your reports. That only covers recommendations sorted into the database's groups of similar findings, so it doesn't prove nothing ever came up twice.

## 3. Findings OIG most often gives other facilities (current inspection program, 112 reports)

These are ranked by how often they appear, not by how serious they are, and they don't predict what OIG will find at El Paso.

| **Communicating test results** (written workflows for each service, monitoring how patients are notified, checking provider compliance) | Four related groups: 21, 12, 9 and 6 of 112 reports | About 140–256 days median where enough items have closed | Not cited for this in your last report. **This is the most common theme.** |

| **Expired supplies / clean supply areas** | 6 of 112 | About 230 days | Close call. Your expired-mask issue was noted but resolved without a recommendation. |
| **Toxic exposure screening navigator roles and oversight** | 4 of 112 | About 189 days | Related to your open rec 2 |

**What other facilities committed to do on test results** (useful if you want to check yourself before OIG does):
- **Shreveport** ([26-00057-170](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-shreveport-healthcare)) wrote workflows for each service, trained staff to a goal of over 90%, and reports compliance to its Quality & Patient Safety Board.
- **Walla Walla** ([24-00599-202](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-jonathan-m-wainwright), closed) audits 30 random charts a month for each service and clinic, with results going to the QPS Council.

**What other facilities committed to do on cleanliness:**
- **Louisville** ([24-03205-235](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-louisville-healthcare), closed) has EMS supervisors inspect at least one area a month, including bed frames under mattresses and exam tables, until it holds 90% for six months. It also dusts sprinkler heads once a year.

## 4. Suggested priorities
1. **Toxic exposure screening (rec 2).** The target date is 2026-12-31. Finish the SOP and gather the monthly CEC data for your closure request.
2. **The two data center items from 2023.** Push OIT for a status. They are the oldest open items on your record.
3. **Self-audit how you communicate test results.** It's the finding OIG gives most often under the current program. Check that every service has a written workflow and that you monitor compliance.
4. **Keep the cleanliness work going.** Have audit data showing it lasted, not just the plan. Re-check the four issues OIG noted without recommendations.

**Caveats from the data:**
- The database sorts recommendations into groups of similar findings by wording or meaning. A group suggests a shared issue but doesn't prove a common cause, and one theme can be split across several groups.
- Read typical closure times alongside how many items have closed. Small groups can show a median of 0 days when items were closed the day the report came out.
- Target dates are each facility's own estimate, so they don't show whether deadlines were missed.
- This data doesn't rate or score facilities.

I can pull the full text of any report or other facilities' complete corrective action plans if that would help.

**Why the missed-deadline rate can't be calculated**

The data source gives this caution: *"A target date is the facility's own estimate. A closure date appears to record when OIG closed the recommendation after reviewing evidence, which can follow the work by months. A closure after the target, or an open recommendation past it, does not show that a facility missed its commitment."*

In other words, if a recommendation closed after its target date, that doesn't prove VHA was late. The facility may have finished on time, and OIG may simply have taken months to review the evidence and close it. Any "missed target" percentage would mostly measure OIG's review time, not VHA's performance.

- The closure-time figures cover 12,164 recommendations, not all 13,014 closed ones. About 6% of closed recommendations, mostly from 2013–2016, have no closure date on OIG's site. Another 11 had closure dates earlier than their publication dates and were left out.
- 946 recommendations closed the day their report came out, probably because they were fixed before publication. These pull the typical closure time down.
- A recommendation assigned to two offices counts for both.

OIG doesn't name a "worst" VA medical center, and I can't give you one either.

**Why OIG doesn't name one**
- OIG doesn't publish rankings, grades or scores that compare facilities. Its reports describe what it found at a specific facility at a specific time and make recommendations to fix those problems.
- The tools I use report what's in OIG's records. They don't rate facilities, and they can't group results by facility.

**Why counting findings wouldn't settle it**
If I added up recommendations for each facility and called the top one "worst," the result would be misleading:
- **Inspections differ.** Facilities are inspected at different times, under different programs, and with different scopes. A larger or more recently inspected facility can have more recommendations just because it got more review.
- **Many reports are triggered by complaints.** Hotline and other special reviews happen because someone reported a problem, so they don't give a balanced comparison across facilities.
- **Recommendations aren't equally serious.** A paperwork gap and a patient safety failure each count as one.
- **Problems get fixed.** Many recommendations have been closed as implemented, so an old count may not reflect how a facility is doing now.

**What I can look up instead**
- **One facility's record:** its OIG reports, open and closed recommendations, and any findings that came up again in later inspections.
- **Problems that show up at many facilities:** how common they are and how long they usually take to fix.
- **Counts and trends:** for example, open recommendations by year, region (VISN), state or topic, and how long recommendations take to close.
- **Specific issues:** for example, suicide prevention or staffing findings, with the report number and link for each.
